end in verb

of a word

also ends in, ending in, end with (a letter), its genitive ends in

classical

Quint. 1.5.62: genetīvō cāsū nōn e litterā, sed tis syllabā terminārentur (Lewis & Short)
Quint. 1.6.7: quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur
Traupman 222, 246

terminor, terminārī, terminātus sum

passive of terminō, with the ablative of the letter, or in + ablative or accusative, conjugation

to end in (a letter or syllable)

The letter goes in the ablative, with its name in apposition: in a litterā terminātur, it ends in the letter a (Traupman 238); cujus genetīvus singulāris in «ae» diphthongō terminātur (Traupman 222).

Other words

  • exeō in + acc. — to end in (a letter)

    also used · classical · Quint. 1.5.61: nē in a quidem atque s litterās exīre temerē masculīna Graeca nōmina … patiēbantur; Quint. 1.6.8: dummodo per eandem litteram in īnfīnītō exeant

    Literally “go out into”: the word runs out into its last letter. Neither Quintilian passage for this phrase is in Lewis & Short or the loci collections, and we have not been able to check them.

Examples

  • omnia, quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur

    all verbs that end in e and o in the indicativeQuint. 1.6.7

  • Prīma dēclīnātiō est nōminis, cujus genetīvus singulāris in «ae» diphthongō terminātur.

    The first declension is of a noun whose genitive singular ends in the diphthong “ae”.Traupman 222

See also ending, letter, declension.
